nature-eecon-136.title: Throughput: the river of matter running through the economy
nature-eecon-136.text:
Textbooks often draw the economy as a closed loop of money passing between firms and households. That circular flow ignores a one-way river underneath it. Throughput is the flow of matter and energy that enters the economy from nature as resources and leaves again as waste and pollution.

Economist {{ref:nature-hist-040}} describes the journey in terms of {{ref:nature-eecon-109}}. Low-entropy resources are taken from nature and turned into goods. Eventually the whole throughput returns to the environment as high-entropy waste. Too large a flow depletes geological capital and damages nature's life-support services.

This makes throughput the quantity that ecological economists want to control. Daly's {{ref:nature-eecon-072}} keeps stocks of capital and people constant with a minimal throughput. {{ref:nature-eecon-143}} mainly aims to cut the material throughput of affluent societies. Technology offers no clean escape: any use of it adds to the cumulative flow of matter and energy, which limits purely technological fixes.

nature-eecon-072.title: The steady-state economy: prosperity without growth
nature-eecon-072.text:
Can an economy be healthy without growing? The steady-state economy says yes. It keeps a constant stock of physical wealth, or capital, and a constant population, so that it does not grow over time. It can apply to a city, a region, a country or the whole world.

The idea updates the classical {{ref:nature-eecon-073}}. Its main champion since the 1970s, {{ref:nature-hist-040}}, added the ecological piece: both stocks are kept constant by a flow of natural resources, the {{ref:nature-eecon-136}}. Both stocks should be as durable as possible. Longer-lasting capital needs a smaller resource flow. A durable population means long lives with low birth and death rates.

The reasoning starts from a picture of the economy as an open subsystem of a finite, non-growing ecosystem. A part cannot grow forever inside a whole that does not grow. That contrasts with the mainstream picture of a closed circular flow between firms and households, with no physical contact with nature.

Daly admits the limits of his own idea. A steady state only postpones, and does not prevent, the eventual exhaustion of minerals. Even sympathetic reviewers in the early 2010s judged it beyond what is politically feasible for now.

nature-eecon-078.title: The declining-state economy: should the economy shrink?
nature-eecon-078.text:
{{ref:nature-hist-044}} thought Daly's {{ref:nature-eecon-072}} did not go far enough. As finite minerals are extracted, he argued, Earth's carrying capacity will fall, so the world economy is heading for collapse. A shrinking economy, not a steady one, would stretch those minerals furthest. He proposed a "minimal bioeconomic program" with restrictions stricter than Daly's.

Daly does not reject a declining path. He sees the steady state as the necessary first step: an economy must stop before it can reverse. Others, including Rifkin, Latouche and Kerschner, argue directly for declining-state strategies, and today's {{ref:nature-eecon-143}} thinkers share the view.

The disagreement is real and unresolved. Steady-state advocates want the economy to stabilize; their more radical allies want it to shrink. Both accept that {{ref:nature-eecon-109}} and finite {{ref:nature-res-209}} stocks set the terms of the argument.

nature-eecon-080.title: Can capitalism stop growing?
nature-eecon-080.text: Radical critics ask whether a steady or shrinking economy can be laid on top of capitalism at all. They point to growth drives built into it: the profit motive, jobs that depend on sales, credit creation by banks and labor-saving technology. Governments need tax revenue from economic activity, and globalization forces countries to compete. Daly disagrees with framing it this way. He holds that the debate between growth and a steady state cuts across the left-right divide. The question remains open.

nature-eecon-074.title: Daly's three institutions for a steady state
nature-eecon-074.text: {{ref:nature-hist-040}} proposed building a {{ref:nature-eecon-072}} by policy, through three state institutions. The first sets minimum and maximum incomes and a maximum on wealth. The second issues transferable reproduction licenses at the replacement fertility level. The third sells depletion quotas that cap the flow of resources. Unlike taxes, quotas directly minimize {{ref:nature-eecon-136}}. Daly calls the mainstream faith that prices and technology can overcome any scarcity "growthmania".

nature-eecon-079.title: Degrowth as the road to a steady state
nature-eecon-079.text: Christian Kerschner argues that rich countries should shrink their economies as a route to a fair world {{ref:nature-eecon-072}}. Shrinking rich economies would leave ecological room for poorer countries to catch up. Kerschner admits a world steady state may stay out of reach, but says such goals can still guide action. Two comparative studies found no analytical difference between Daly's steady-state economics and European {{ref:nature-eecon-143}}.

nature-eecon-084.title: The Great Stagnation: a critique of degrowth
nature-eecon-084.text: Wim Naudé argues that Western economies already look like {{ref:nature-eecon-143}}. They are in a "Great Stagnation" of falling innovation and entrepreneurship. In prolonged stagnation, he notes, the economy increasingly works like a zero-sum system, where one person's gain is another's loss. His critique disputes the benefits claimed for {{ref:nature-eecon-079}} and the steady state.

nature-eecon-082.title: Overdevelopment: when rich countries have too much
nature-eecon-082.text: Development is usually something poor countries lack. Overdevelopment turns that around: the rich countries of the global north are too developed, which increases humanity's ecological impact and causes problems for rich and poor countries alike. The idea comes from Leopold Kohr's 1977 book The Overdeveloped Nations, which was mainly about {{ref:nature-eecon-185}}.

nature-eecon-075.title: The solar-income budget: living on sunlight
nature-eecon-075.text: Before industrialization, people lived within what {{ref:nature-hist-040}} calls a solar-income budget. Daly sees two sources of wealth. One is a stock of minerals, which we can extract as fast as we choose. The other is a flow of solar energy that is beyond our control. Since the Sun will keep shining for billions of years, the mineral stock is the crucial scarcity. The Industrial Revolution broke the budget by extracting minerals at a rapidly increasing rate.

nature-eecon-124.title: Post-normal science: when facts are uncertain and stakes are high
nature-eecon-124.text: Some decisions cannot wait for certainty. Post-normal science is a problem-solving approach for science used in policy when "facts are uncertain, values in dispute, stakes high and decisions urgent". Silvio Funtowicz and Jerome Ravetz developed it in the 1990s. In such cases it sets aside the traditional ideal of truth and focuses on quality, checked by internal and extended peer communities. Its diagram plots system uncertainties against decision stakes, separating applied science, professional consultancy and post-normal science. It complements risk analysis and {{ref:nature-val-001}} rather than replacing them. It is meant for pandemics, ecosystem collapse, biodiversity loss and the shift to sustainability. In modeling it favors "models to map our ignorance about the future" over models to predict it. Critics say it adds nothing new, turns climate scientists into "stealth advocates" and undermines empiricism.

nature-eecon-101.title: Emergy ratios: judging how a process uses resources
nature-eecon-101.text: {{ref:nature-eecon-099}} accounting produces ratios that judge how a process uses local, renewable and purchased resources. The emergy yield ratio (EYR) measures how far an investment lets a process exploit local resources. The environmental loading ratio (ELR) compares non-renewable and imported emergy with renewable emergy, signaling stress on ecosystems. The emergy sustainability index (ESI) is EYR divided by ELR.

nature-eecon-100.title: Transformity: how much sunlight a joule costs
nature-eecon-100.text: If 10,000 solar emjoules are needed to make a joule of wood, the wood's solar transformity is 10,000 seJ/J. Transformity is the {{ref:nature-eecon-099}} needed per unit of available energy produced, and so a measure of energy quality. Sunlight absorbed by the Earth has a solar transformity of 1.0 by definition. Odum's 1975 table of "energy quality factors" first stated the principle behind it: quality is measured by the energy used in transformations.

nature-eecon-088.title: Vienna and Barcelona: two ways to measure social metabolism
nature-eecon-088.text: Two schools measure {{ref:nature-eecon-086}}. Both build on material flow accounting, which tracks a state's or region's inputs and outputs of materials and energy, imports and exports included. The Vienna school's MEFA, founded by Marina Fischer-Kowalski, studies national economies over time and standardizes data for comparison. The Barcelona school's {{ref:nature-eecon-123}}, built around Mario Giampietro and Kozo Mayumi, studies subsectors of present economies with tailor-made accounts within a set "grammar".

nature-eecon-123.title: MuSIASEM: accounting across scales
nature-eecon-123.text: MuSIASEM, Multi-Scale Integrated Analysis of Societal and Ecosystem Metabolism, is an accounting method for social-ecological systems that can simulate possible development paths. It keeps assessments consistent across scales and across economic, demographic and energy measures in different units. It tracks who uses which resources and why, the environmental pressures that result, and how far needs and pressures are shifted abroad through trade. Mario Giampietro and Kozo Mayumi created it around 1997 at the Autonomous University of Barcelona. It suits the nexus of food, energy, water and land, and has been tested with the FAO.

nature-eecon-087.title: Hunters, farmers, industry: three sociometabolic regimes
nature-eecon-087.text: Rolf Sieferle divided human history into three regimes by main energy source. Hunter-gatherers relied on "passive solar energy" from recent photosynthesis, giving nomadic societies with few people per area. The Neolithic Revolution brought an agrarian regime of "active solar energy use": forests cleared for farms, settled life and faster {{ref:nature-eecon-202}}. The industrial regime runs on fossil fuels. Historians reconstruct this using indicators such as Total Primary Energy Supply and Human Appropriation of Net Primary Production (HANPP).

nature-eecon-122.title: Eco-urbanism: closing the city's loops
nature-eecon-122.text: Eco-urbanism tries to heal the {{ref:nature-eecon-120}} at city scale. It brings a city's energy, water, food and waste flows back within its own systems. The aim is greater self-reliance through "closed-loop systems" that reduce dependence on outside networks. Critics link it to "managerial environmentalism" and doubt that sustainable cities are possible within global capitalism.

nature-eecon-121.title: Jason Moore's rival reading of the metabolic rift
nature-eecon-121.text: Jason W. Moore dates metabolic rifts to the birth of capitalism in the "long" 16th century, recurring in every phase of its development. He traces them to capitalist relations based on the law of value, not to industrial agriculture. Moore holds that splitting social from natural systems is empirically false and arbitrary. James O'Connor adds that capitalism's undervaluing of nature leads to economic crisis, a "second contradiction of capitalism". Moore's view diverges widely from Foster's on what causes ecological crisis.

nature-eecon-134.title: Declining terms of trade: coffee buys less every year
nature-eecon-134.text: Working for the UN Economic Commission for Latin America, Raúl Prebisch saw that exports such as coffee and copper bought fewer manufactured goods over time. Prices of raw materials from poorer countries fall relative to the manufactures they import. His ideas founded dependency theory and import substitution industrialization. A recent study estimated that {{ref:nature-eecon-133}} may have reduced North–South convergence by 34% across 43 countries between 2000 and 2014.

nature-eecon-139.title: Coevolutionary economics: pests, pesticides and the rules between
nature-eecon-139.text: Pests evolve resistance to pesticides, pesticides change, and the institutions regulating them change too. Richard Norgaard used that story to bring coevolution into ecological economics. The idea began in biology for two species evolving together, then grew into gene-culture coevolution. Coevolutionary economics studies change as mutual feedback and selection among social, environmental and economic systems. Ecological economics itself is defined by this coevolution of economies and ecosystems. Norgaard and Giorgos Kallis applied it to water development, urbanization and rural communities.

nature-eecon-137.title: The materials balance principle: everything goes somewhere
nature-eecon-137.text: The materials balance principle applies {{ref:nature-eecon-094}} to the economy: everything that goes in comes out as product, stock or waste. {{ref:nature-eecon-019}} rests on it plus a systems approach. Mass balance makes sure waste and by-products are not overlooked, whereas economic input-output tables often leave them out because they have no economic value. Allen Kneese, {{ref:nature-hist-071}} and Ralph d'Arge set out a "materials balance approach" in 1970. The principle traveled from Lavoisier's chemistry into chemical engineering and then environmental science.

nature-eecon-131.title: The maximum power principle: winning by using more energy
nature-eecon-131.text: {{ref:nature-hist-063}} proposed that organisms, ecosystems and societies organize themselves to maximize their use of available energy for survival. Societies with access to higher-quality energy, he held, had an advantage in the evolutionary struggle. In {{ref:nature-eecon-130}}, the principle of maximum power efficiency takes central place: the most advantageous function occurs when the environmental load matches the system's internal resistance.

nature-eecon-138.title: How big should the economy be?
nature-eecon-138.text: Alongside fair distribution and efficient allocation, ecological economics asks a third question: how large should the economy be relative to the ecosystems it depends on? In a "full-world economy", the ecological costs of more growth may exceed its immediate social benefits. Daly sees the {{ref:nature-eecon-072}} as a first step, after which society must decide whether the optimum lies above or below present levels. He judges we have overshot it, while conceding the optimum is difficult, probably impossible, to define. Martínez Alier adds that as the economy grows, poor people lose access to environmental resources and bear an outsized share of pollution.

nature-eecon-125.title: The extended peer community: more voices checking the science
nature-eecon-125.text: In {{ref:nature-eecon-124}}, scientists are not the only ones checking the quality of the science behind a decision. A wider group of stakeholders shares the task. Participants are not passive learners waiting for experts to convince them; they resolve issues through debate. Because these spaces carry differing values and unequal power, agreement is not guaranteed. Some argue conservation science, with its many layers of policy-makers and stakeholders, has always worked this way.

nature-eecon-092.title: Green logistics: moving goods with less harm
nature-eecon-092.text: Green logistics measures and reduces the environmental impact of moving and storing goods, information and services. It began in the mid-1980s and seeks to balance economic and environmental efficiency. Small choices matter: packaging decides how many items fit in a container, and so strongly shapes CO2 emissions per product moved. Cleaner options can be costly. Ammonia is 3-7 times more expensive than traditional marine fuels.

nature-eecon-126.title: Numbers for post-normal science
nature-eecon-126.text: {{ref:nature-eecon-124}} has its own quantitative tools: NUSAP for numbers, sensitivity auditing for indicators and models, quantitative storytelling, and {{ref:nature-eecon-123}}. It gives "garbage in, garbage out" a pointed meaning: the case where input uncertainties must be hidden, lest model outputs become completely indeterminate.

reviews.ecological-economics: The chapter's thread is physics. Because energy is conserved and {{ref:nature-eecon-109}} always tends to rise, every economy is a {{ref:nature-eecon-136}} of matter and energy: low-entropy resources in, high-entropy waste out. That is why ecological economists count {{ref:nature-eecon-095}}, {{ref:nature-eecon-110}} and {{ref:nature-eecon-102}}, and why falling energy returns worry them. It is also why they separate growth from development, warn of {{ref:nature-eecon-090}}, and propose a {{ref:nature-eecon-072}} that holds capital and population constant. Critics answer that technology and substitution have kept growth going, and debates over degrowth, valuation and unequal exchange remain open.
